related_questions.question: How long can a person with HIV live?

text_blocks.snippet: With consistent antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV can live a long and healthy life, with a life expectancy comparable to those without HIV. Without treatment, however, HIV can progress to AIDS within a few years, significantly shortening life expectancy.
snippet_highlighted_words: With consistent antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV can live a long and healthy life, with a life expectancy comparable to those without HIV

list.title: Early Treatment is Key:
list.snippet: Prompt initiation of ART significantly improves long-term health outcomes for people with HIV.

list.title: Life Expectancy Similar to General Population:
list.snippet: Studies show that people with HIV who start ART early and maintain consistent treatment can have a life expectancy close to that of the general population. For example, one study found that people with high CD4 counts (above 500) who started ART after 2015 had a life expectancy similar to the general population.

list.title: Factors Affecting Life Expectancy:
list.snippet: Several factors can influence life expectancy, including the stage of HIV at diagnosis, access to and adherence to ART, and other health conditions.

list.title: Untreated HIV:
list.snippet: Without treatment, HIV progresses through stages, eventually leading to AIDS. The progression can vary, but without treatment, life expectancy is significantly reduced.

list.title: Aging with HIV:
list.snippet: With the advancements in HIV treatment, people with HIV are living longer and experiencing the effects of aging, similar to the general population.

list.title: Importance of Ongoing Care:
list.snippet: Regular monitoring, including CD4 counts and viral load tests, is crucial to ensure the effectiveness of ART and to manage any other health issues that may arise.

related_questions.question: What is the best drink for HIV patients?

text_blocks.snippet: For people living with HIV, water is the best drink, followed by unsweetened juices and other hydrating beverages. Staying well-hydrated is crucial for overall health, especially when managing HIV, as it helps reduce medication side effects and prevents dehydration, which can exacerbate other health conditions.
snippet_highlighted_words: water is the best drink, followed by unsweetened juices and other hydrating beverages

list.title: Importance:
list.snippet: Water helps the body function properly, aids in digestion, and can help flush out medications. It also helps prevent dehydration, which can lead to fatigue and other complications.

list.title: Amount:
list.snippet: Aim for 8-10 glasses (64-80 ounces) of water per day, or more if experiencing diarrhea, vomiting, or fever.

list.title: Quality:
list.snippet: If the water source is questionable, boil it for 10 minutes and let it cool down before drinking, or use a water filter.

list.title: Considerations:
list.snippet: Unsweetened carbonated or flavored waters are also fine, but avoid sugary drinks that can contribute to weight gain.

list.title: Juices:
list.snippet: Freshly squeezed or unsweetened juices can provide additional vitamins and nutrients, but be mindful of added sugars.

list.title: Soups:
list.snippet: Clear broths and vegetable soups can help with hydration, especially if experiencing nausea or diarrhea.

list.title: Electrolyte drinks:
list.snippet: If experiencing significant fluid loss due to diarrhea or vomiting, consider drinks like Gatorade to replenish electrolytes.

list.title: Herbal Teas:
list.snippet: Certain herbal teas can be soothing and hydrating, but avoid those with caffeine, which can be dehydrating.
Sugary drinks: Sodas, sweetened juices, and other sugary beverages can lead to weight gain and other health problems.
Alcoholic beverages: Alcohol can dehydrate the body and interfere with HIV medications.
Caffeinated beverages: Coffee and some teas can also have a dehydrating effect.
Milk products: If experiencing diarrhea, consider limiting or avoiding milk products temporarily to see if it improves your symptoms.
Listen to your body: Pay attention to your thirst cues and drink when you feel thirsty.
Eat smaller, more frequent meals: This can help with nausea and vomiting and ensure you're getting enough nutrients and fluids.

Consult with a healthcare professional: If you have any concerns about your hydration or diet, consult with your HIV healthcare provider or a registered dietitian for personalized recommendations, according to HIV.gov.

text_blocks.snippet: By prioritizing water and other hydrating beverages, people living with HIV can support their overall health and well-being.

related_questions.question: What happens to your body when you are HIV positive?
related_questions.snippet: HIV damages the immune system so that the body is less able to fight infection and disease. If HIV isn't treated, it can take years before it weakens the immune system enough to become AIDS . Thanks to treatment, most people in the U.S. don't get AIDS .

related_questions.question: Is it possible to sleep with an HIV positive person and not be infected?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, it is possible to sleep with an HIV-positive person and not be infected with HIV, particularly if the HIV-positive person is on effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) and has an undetectable viral load. When someone with HIV achieves and maintains an undetectable viral load, the risk of sexual transmission of HIV is effectively zero, according to the CDC.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, it is possible to sleep with an HIV-positive person and not be infected with HIV

list.title: Undetectable Viral Load:
list.snippet: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses the virus to undetectable levels in the blood. When this happens, the virus cannot be transmitted through sexual contact.

list.title: PARTNER Studies:
list.snippet: The PARTNER studies, which followed thousands of couples where one partner was HIV-positive and the other was HIV-negative, found no instances of HIV transmission when the positive partner had an undetectable viral load, says Aidsmap.

list.title: PrEP:
list.snippet: For individuals at high risk of HIV exposure, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) can be used to further reduce the risk of infection. PrEP is a medication that can be taken to prevent HIV acquisition, says NHS inform.

list.title: Other Considerations:
list.snippet: While the risk of transmission is effectively zero with an undetectable viral load, it's still important to consider other factors, such as the potential for other STIs, and to discuss these with a healthcare provider.
